# Out of the Lab and Into the Factory

PT—00/ 05

# Out of the Lab and Into the Factory

The New Computers, and the Mission for Quantum Hardware

![Fifth Solvay Conference on Physics, 1927](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-000.jpg)

 PT—1

**[FIG.1]** Solvay Conference — 1927 The founders of quantum theory

PT—01/ 05

## Introduction

Special thanks to [John Martinis](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2025/martinis/facts/), [Florian Schreck](https://www.strontiumbec.com/), and [Dylan Sabulsky](https://scholar.google.co.uk/citations?user=5faRM7kAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao), out of whose detailed correspondence has this vision been formed.

## 1. Introduction

Quantum computing is at risk of becoming an embarrassing footnote in the history of technology.

If you've spent time around the field, you know the elephant in the room; on the one hand, futuristic looking computers the size of entire rooms, and on the other, fuzzy and opaque explanations of their supposed practical utility. Shor's algorithm

![Peter Shor at the Dirac Medal Award Ceremony, 2017](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-peter-shor.jpg)

 **Shor's algorithm, 1994** An algorithm native to quantum computers that finds the largest prime factors of a given number exponentially faster than classical computers. Discovered and proposed by American mathematician Peter Shor. (famous for the threat it poses to modern day encryption systems) has been known since 1994, yet over 3 decades later the largest number it has ever factored is 35. And that was 7 years ago^[1](https://juser.fz-juelich.de/record/1042431/files/NIC_2025_Willsch.pdf).

In that same timeframe, the world was introduced to reusable rockets, self-driving cars, mass-market artificial intelligence and implantable brain–computer interfaces. It is by no means obvious that these fields are any less technically demanding than quantum computing.

Progress in other fields has been exponential, while quantum processing power has barely changed. Why?

The lack of external accountability made the industry complacent.

To say that quantum computing has made *no* progress would be too harsh; some of the world's most gifted scientists have produced extraordinary results controlling individual atoms, photons, electrons and superconducting circuits. But the field is so specialised, and knowledge so hopelessly siloed between sub-fields, that almost nobody can practically judge the aggregate progress.

Those allocating capital are left with no choice but to let companies mark their own homework.

![Theodore Maiman with the first working laser](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-laser.jpg)

**[FIG.2]** Theodore Maiman First working laser — 1960

There is a better way.

Lasers moved from an unproven proposal to product in 4 years^[2](https://www.photonics.com/LinearChart.aspx?ChartID=2).
The SR-71 Blackbird went from idea to test flight in a similar time frame^[3](https://www.lockheedmartin.com/en-us/news/features/history/blackbird.html).
Why can’t incumbent computer manufacturers simply do the same?

Leading quantum companies are home to some of the world’s most brilliant scientists and engineers, but their industrial infrastructure and manufacturing supply chains were conceived of and constructed in a different century.

Physically speaking, the supply chain that a quantum computer depends upon consists of semiconductor fabs, lasers, chemical epitaxy, packaging, control electronics and either cryogenics or ultra-high vacuum systems.

Someone has to be responsible for physically making these components, and the capability to do so is scattered across a small number of specialist suppliers and often between jurisdictions. Even the largest companies control only a small part of this chain, and any new part or process incurs lead times measured in months or even years.

This traps companies in a simple loop:

> Long lead times mean few builds, having few builds forces years' worth of upgrades into each machine, more improvements per build demands yet more planning and de-risking, and the next build takes even longer.

We at Pathfinder are developing quantum computers in a new way, but we are only one company. If quantum computing is ever to be more than a mere embarrassing technological footnote, the entire industry must escape from academia’s bureaucratic overhang, slash development costs and lead times, and start building complete systems instead of ever-narrower pieces of them.

PT—02/ 05

Quantum Computing inherited an institutional model designed to produce demonstrations over products.

## How Did We Get Here?

![Atomic physics experiment — University of Amsterdam](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/uva-atomic-01.jpg)

 PT—2

## 2. How Did We Get Here?

Quantum Computing inherited an institutional model designed to produce demonstrations over products.

![Crowded optical bench with lasers, mirrors, and cabling](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-optical-bench.jpg)

**[FIG.3]** Ultracold-atom optical table — UQUAM / MPQ © Immanuel Bloch — European Commission

The journey began as a sequence of experiments conducted in University physics departments all over the world.

Not long after Peter Shor’s discovery of his eponymous prime factorisation algorithm, researchers at NIST demonstrated the world’s first quantum logic operation. In 1998, a team from Oxford ran one of the first complete quantum algorithms on a two-qubit machine.

These first computers were not products in the way one may think of an iPhone or a Tesla - that is, mass-produced factory-line items - rather they were one-off experimental setups assembled by hand. Many of these experiments were built as PhD projects and postdoctoral research, and with that came academic incentive structures, timelines, and purchasing habits.

Take the NIST experiment described above. The first quantum logic gate was reported in a four-page paper

![First page of Monroe et al., Demonstration of a Fundamental Quantum Logic Gate, Physical Review Letters, 1995](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-nist-paper.jpg)

 **Monroe et al., 1995** Phys. Rev. Lett. 75, 4714 — the NIST demonstration of a controlled-NOT gate on a single trapped beryllium ion. Four pages of states, pulses, results and error sources. containing the atomic states used, the laser-pulse sequence, the measured result and the sources of error.

Notice, however, what was left out.

- Bill of materials — not included

- Assembly time — not included

- Supplier list — not included

- Maintenance procedure — not included

- Account of the earlier versions which failed — not included

**None of this was required to substantiate the scientific claim.**

This distinction is written into the way academic research is assessed. In 2023, a House of Commons inquiry found that publication in a journal was the expected outcome of almost all academic research in Britain^[13](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmselect/cmsctech/101/report.html). The standard academic CV, the committee was told, consisted principally of publications, grants and invitations to speak, while the Research Excellence Framework assessed published work according to its “originality, significance and rigour.”

Assembly time and fabrication yield appear nowhere in the scorecard.

**...But it couldn’t have happened any other way.**

Before the question of mass-manufacturing a quantum computer made any sense to ask, Wolfgang Paul

![Portrait of Wolfgang Paul](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-wolfgang-paul.jpg)

 **Wolfgang Paul, 1913–1993** German physicist who invented the Paul trap — using oscillating electric fields to confine charged particles in free space. Shared the 1989 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work, which became the foundation of trapped-ion quantum computing. first had to discover that oscillating electric fields could confine ions in free space. David Wineland

![Portrait of David Wineland](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-david-wineland.jpg)

 **David Wineland, b. 1944** American physicist at NIST whose group showed that trapped ions could be laser-cooled nearly to rest. Shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physics; his laboratory later demonstrated the first quantum logic gate on a single ion. ’s 1978 group in Colorado had to prove that trapped ions could be cooled using laser light. Only after another seventeen years of work did the first quantum logic gate follow.

Without the work done by these pioneers, the industry would never have gotten started. The early emphasis on proving isolated pieces of the machine was entirely appropriate, because nobody yet knew whether those pieces could be made to work at all.

Thirty years of experiments later and many of these early doubts have been allayed: quantum logic gates are now routine, processors with more than a thousand physical qubits have been built, and error-corrected logical qubits have begun to improve as more physical qubits are added.

...But what makes a good prototype isn't always what makes a good product.

Innovation is followed by manufacture, and quantum computing is now beginning this transition for itself. The National Academies described the field’s greatest challenge in 2019 as moving “from an understanding of the basic science to the creation of useful devices.”

Unluckily for the budding researcher, this is a significantly less glamorous process than finding the one great scientific breakthrough. Luckily, however, we already have a role model whom we can follow: every other technological industry in existence.

Innovation is followed by manufacture.

PT—03/ 05

 High unit cost and long lead times are the predictable result of producing highly specialised equipment in small volumes.

## The Industry Today

![Optical table atomic physics experiment — University of Amsterdam](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/uva-atomic-02.jpg)

 PT—3

## 3. The Industry Today

Now, more than 30 years later, the technology attracts industrial quantities of capital. In 2025 alone, companies across quantum computing, sensing and communications raised $4.9 billion^[5](https://quantumconsortium.org/publication/2026-state-of-the-global-quantum-industry-report/) in venture capital, while governments announced another $12.7 billion^[5](https://quantumconsortium.org/publication/2026-state-of-the-global-quantum-industry-report/) in funding commitments. The Quantum Economic Development Consortium counted 556^[5](https://quantumconsortium.org/publication/2026-state-of-the-global-quantum-industry-report/) specialist companies operating worldwide.

Despite this, The MIT Quantum Index identified that the number of companies developing an announced, prototype or commercial quantum processor in 2025 was fewer than eighty^[6](https://qir.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/MIT-QIR-2025.pdf). Only around two dozen^[6](https://qir.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/MIT-QIR-2025.pdf) offered one commercially. Hundreds of companies, billions of dollars and several national programmes therefore depend upon **fewer than one hundred organisations attempting to build the central machine^[6](https://qir.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/MIT-QIR-2025.pdf).**

Those manufacturers, in turn, depend upon a supply chain still organised around individual scientific experiments.

In 2023 the National Quantum Computing Centre bought two strontium-ion laser suites from TOPTICA for £640,810^[7](https://www.sell2wales.gov.wales/search/show/search_view.aspx?ID=NOV457942). Each contained eight lasers, together with the control electronics, frequency-locking equipment, optical fibres, software and rack required to operate them. The contract allowed nine months between order and delivery.

Why so much? Why so slow?

Laser companies are stuck between a rock and a hard place. All orders are bespoke; the laser system for a Strontium-based quantum computer might have little in common with the laser system for a Calcium-based atom physics experiment, and who’s to say what the next order will be?

High unit cost and long lead times are the predictable result of producing highly specialised equipment in small volumes.

Fragment the demand that way and economies of scale never appear. A manufacturer serving several dozen laboratories, all of whom have different requirements, cannot amortise an automated production line, while a quantum company working against the available catalogue gives the supplier little reason to redesign it. Long lead times, high prices and by-hand integration then appear to be intrinsic properties of the technology rather than consequences of the production methods being used.

More money thrown around in grants is unlikely to solve the problem. It would be foolish to assume that the difficulty is one of being insufficiently clever to use the toolkit we have; the sharper question is whether the toolkit itself is up to the task.

![Drone photo of Intel Fab 9 under construction in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, January 2024](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-gordian-v2.jpg)

 PT—4

**[FIG.5]** Intel Fab 9 — Rio Rancho, New Mexico Advanced packaging facility, January 2024

## Cutting the Gordian Knot

## 4. Cutting the Gordian Knot

 1. The Idiot Index 2. Question Every Requirement 3. Standardised Components 4. Vertical Integration 5. Increase Iteration Speed

Junior engineers are explicitly told that requirements from "smart people" are the most dangerous, because nobody thinks to question them.

Is there any historical precedent for having solved these problems?

As it turns out there is. SpaceX is the most relevant example, despite aerospace engineering and quantum hardware not having much in common at first glance.

> What is a rocket made of? Aerospace-grade aluminum alloys, plus some titanium, copper, and carbon fiber. And then I asked, what is the value of those materials on the commodity market? It turned out that the materials cost of a rocket was around 2 percent of the typical price—which is a crazy ratio for a large mechanical product. 8 Two percent . Your car’s raw materials are maybe 20-30% of sticker price. Consumer electronics are similar. But rockets? Ninety-eight cents of every dollar was going somewhere other than what it was made of. Where? Three places, it seems. Supplier markups stacking through contract layers, each tier adding 15-30% margin. Custom designs that couldn’t achieve manufacturing scale. Expendable hardware thrown away after every flight. None of these are the laws of physics. Traditional aerospace treated high costs as fixed constraints. But what if you treated them as variables? How do you actually capture that 98%? 9

The negative feedback loop is the same in both cases: low volumes keep components bespoke; bespoke production offers little incentive for production overhaul; prices remain high and lead times long; and low volumes persist. In one case, the scarce unit is a launch. In the other, it is a computer.

It's the same problem, and it has been solved before.

Quantum hardware comes with its own constraints: unsettled architectures, extreme tolerances and components produced in tiny volumes. So is the resemblance merely superficial, or does quantum computing face the same underlying supply-chain problem that SpaceX confronted? If it does, what were the specific practices, manufacturing strategy and organisational principles that allowed SpaceX to break the cycle, and which of them could work here?

![Engineers examining hardware wreckage](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-002.jpg)

**[FIG.6]** Early SpaceX Launch site, 2006 Debris of the Falcon 1 launch

### 1. The Idiot Index

Musk eventually named this the “idiot index”: the ratio of the actual cost of a part to the cost of its raw materials. “If the ratio is high,” he says, “you’re an idiot.”

A classical computer is constructed from specific component parts: GPUs, CPUs, cooling systems, et cetera. A quantum computer is much the same; high-precision lasers, vacuum systems, single-photon detectors, and more.

> Consider the Falcon 1 actuator. A vendor quoted $120,000 and eighteen months of development time. SpaceX engineer Steve Davis built it in-house in nine months for $3,900 10 .

Each of these component parts can be assigned it’s own idiot index; a high value is a flashing light pointing to a poorly optimised manufacturing process. Values for ultra-precision components will be higher than those for parts with lower precision requirements, but this only indicates a higher cost floor; it says nothing about how far the current machinery is above it.

![Idiot index estimates for eight quantum computing components: vacuum chamber 25×, dilution fridge 7×, ECDL 30×, optical mount 50×, SPAD module 60×, acousto-optic modulator 45×, RF control system 50×, MOCVD reactor 20×](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-idiot-index.jpg)

### 2. Question Every Requirement

Junior engineers are explicitly told that requirements from “smart people” are the most dangerous, because nobody thinks to question them.

A high idiot index identifies an expensive component; the knee-jerk response is ask how the component can be manufactured more cheaply, but **the more astute question is to ask whether it needs to exist at all**. Get rid of the part entirely, and the idiot index falls to 0.

> Delete, delete, delete... the best part is no part - the best process is no process.

The same exercise can be carried into the quantum supply chain. Commercial MOCVD reactors

![Commercial MOCVD reactor used for epitaxial semiconductor growth](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-mocvd.jpg)

 **MOCVD Reactor** Metal-organic chemical vapour deposition — a machine that grows thin semiconductor layers by flowing precursor gases over a heated wafer. are designed to grow semiconductor layers of all different chemical makeups and sizes, all with fully automated handling.

How much of the cost and complexity of the machine could be reduced if the requirement to fit multiple designs was removed? A refurbished second-hand reactor cost Glasgow University £165,000 in 2017^[11](https://www.publiccontractsscotland.gov.uk/search/show/search_view.aspx?ID=JUL290649), while high-capacity commercial systems have historically cost millions^[12](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20130416PD214.html).

### 3. Standardised Components

The existing approach was bespoke vehicles per mission. **SpaceX bet the opposite: that cost savings from standardisation would exceed the value of customisation.** Yes, customers wanted custom solutions. But they wanted low prices even more. Force them to choose, and they’d adapt.

Go to any quantum hardware supplier right now, be it lasers, vacuum chambers or semiconductor fabs, and you will inevitably see the words ‘request a quotation’ in place of a price tag. Why is this? Are suppliers being secretive, or do they genuinely not know?

![Two ways to buy the same laser: a long request-a-quotation specification form, or a listed price with a five-day delivery and a buy button](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-laser-quote.jpg)

It’s the latter, of course: it’s the same low-volume-differing-requirements problem again. **Economies of scale only emerge from making the same design in bulk; fragmented demand denies suppliers the opportunity to do so.**

### 4. Vertical Integration

Vertical integration gives manufacturers the freedom to cut everything that is not absolutely critical to building better computers.

This means avoiding the time cost and incurred margins of outsourcing components, but it comes with costs of its own. Fixed costs, specifically. Bringing the machines in-house isn’t cheap, and incurs a lot of complexity in the short term. In fact, if the goal is to build a single computer, it doesn’t make much sense to bring the manufacturing in-house at all.

> If materials are cheap and the tax is all process and overhead, you need to control the process to capture the savings. You can’t negotiate your way to a 10x cost reduction with suppliers who have profits baked in at every tier. By building 80% of its hardware internally, SpaceX collapsed the traditional aerospace stack.

### 5. Increase Iteration Speed

Traditional aerospace builds few prototypes, each one expensive and near-flight-ready. SpaceX builds many cheaper prototypes. **They’d rather have ten rough versions to blow up than one polished version they’re afraid to break.**

The idiot index identifies where manufacturing optimisations can be made, vertical integration gives the control needed to implement them, and standardising the components unlocks the economies of scale needed to make them cheap.

But internalising all these manufacturing processes internalises the maintenance costs, not to mention the price of the machines themselves. The factory loses money every second that these machines aren’t producing something valuable. Iteration speed is what makes the whole process profitable - new ideas can be tested cheaply, quickly, and the manufacturers needn’t be precious about whether an idea is likely to work or not. The whole design process gets flipped on its head; instead of having to meticulously plan out what ideas get to go in the new design before starting manufacture, ideas can be tested cheaply and quickly. If they don’t work, the time and financial loss is minimal.

![Evolution of the Raptor engine from version 1 to 3](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-003.jpg)

**[FIG.7]** Evolution of the Raptor engine, from version 1 to 3 Simplify, simplify, simplify!

All these parts came together in a way that was mutually reinforcing; first-principles engineering identified manufacturing optimisations, vertical integration let those optimisations happen, standardisation facilitated the high production rate that led to so many test flights.

 1. The Idiot Index 2. Question Every Requirement 3. Standardised Components 4. Vertical Integration 5. Increase Iteration Speed

![The Traitorous Eight at Fairchild Semiconductor, 1960](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-noyce.jpg)

**[FIG.8]** The Traitorous Eight Fairchild Semiconductor, 1960

PT—05/ 05

## The Window

## 5. The Window

In every new industry, there is a short window where a small handful of people decide the shape of the coming decades.

![Steve Wozniak seated at an Apple II keyboard while Steve Jobs works on an open machine beside him](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/fig-jobs-woz.jpg)

**[FIG.9]** Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs Apple Computer, Cupertino — 1977

At the dawn of every major technology, there was a short window in which the work of a few people decided how the field would take shape for decades to come. Jobs and Wozniak in the seventies, Bezos and Page in the nineties, OpenAI and Anthropic today. Tomorrow, the window for quantum computing will close, but who closes it remains to be seen.

Pathfinder is looking for a technical cofounder. An engineer with the talent and the nerve to hack together quantum computers from scratch.

# Diamond QPU v2.1

v2.1 · ODMR

# Diamond QPU

Thanks to [Dr. Jason Smith](https://www.materials.ox.ac.uk/peoplepages/smithj.html), [Dr. Joe A. Smith](https://www.sheffield.ac.uk/eee/people/academic-staff/joe-smith), and [Dr. Chong Zu](https://artsci.washu.edu/faculty-staff/chong-zu) for their review and continued correspondence.

Designed as a compact tabletop system for a conventional lab without extensive infrastructure. **Our chief objective is to manufacture a complete quantum computer as quickly and cost-effectively as possible.**

## System architecture

![Pathfinder Diamond QPU: diamond NV chiplet flip-chip bonded to a microwave and RF ASIC, optically coupled to a silicon nitride photonic circuit for 515 nm excitation and fluorescence collection.](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/diamond-qpu-architecture.png)

Qubits are housed in a 4x4x0.5 mm ⟨111⟩ diamond plate, with an NV depth ~100 nanometers. An ASIC flip-chip bonded to the diamond delivers microwave and RF and carries silicon photonics for 515 nm excitation and fluorescence collection. Pauli X, Y, Z and entangling gates are driven by pulses applied to the various spins. The diamond is cooled by a triple Peltier stack.

## 1. Diamond register

The register is housed in a 4 x 4 x 0.5 mm synthetic diamond plate, sourced from Diatope in Germany. Target NV depth is approximately 100 nm below the diamond surface.

⟨111⟩ diamond is preferred. That orientation simplifies the optical geometry for an appropriately aligned NV.

The desired register contains a nitrogen vacancy surrounded by eight sufficiently strongly coupled ^13C nuclear spins. Those spins are the qubits: Pauli X, Y and Z, and the entangling gates between them, are microwave and RF pulses applied to that register.

Increasing ^13C abundance increases the probability of obtaining a useful nuclear register, while also increasing the surrounding spin bath (reducing electron-spin coherence time). The final isotopic composition will be selected from experimental data rather than assumed in advance.

## 2. NV creation and characterisation

The diamond is implanted with ^14N and annealed by Diatope, who also handle characterisation.

The diamond is then characterized to identify an NV with:

**Stable fluorescence:** We prepare the NV into the NV^− charge state. It must produce a repeatable fluorescence count rate under repeated 515 nm excitation, without significant blinking or charge-state switching. The acceptance threshold will be set from measured photon-count statistics during characterization.

**Electron coherence:** we target Hahn-echo T_2 ≳ 1 ms, comparable to the ~1.18 ms electron-spin coherence demonstrated in similar NV registers in the literature. Note that at our target ~100 nm depth, this is a prospective lower bound and may be far higher.

**Individually addressable hyperfine couplings:** resonant frequencies of the in-register ^13C spins must be sufficiently isolated such that driving one nuclear spin does not rotate another. Our engineering target is ≥99.9% fidelity for a single-qubit Bloch rotation, corresponding to ≤10^−3 total error from crosstalk and control imperfections.

## 3. ASIC antenna and flip-chip bonding

On-diamond metallisation is replaced by an ASIC. The ASIC is flip-chip bonded onto the diamond plate. It carries microwave and RF delivery to the electron and nuclear spins, and it carries the photonic circuit that excites the NV and collects its fluorescence.

Silicon photonics is fundamental to the architecture. 515 nm excitation is coupled into waveguides on the ASIC; phonon-sideband fluorescence is collected on the same chip and routed to the detector.

Flip-chip bonding places the selected NV in the microwave/RF field and in the optical mode of the photonic circuit. Every Pauli rotation and every entangling gate is a pulse sent through this ASIC into those spins. Bump geometry, trace layout, waveguide alignment and the required field at the NV are fixed after simulation and bonding trials.

## 4. Static magnetic field

A static magnetic field of approximately 40 mT is applied along the selected NV axis. This follows the architecture used in closely related Delft multi-spin NV experiments, which operate at approximately 403–404 G.

The field is generated using a permanent neodymium magnet mounted beside the Peltier stack on a precision translation stage. Delft uses a similar arrangement with a temperature-stabilized permanent magnet on a piezo stage.

Alignment is performed by recording the NV’s ODMR spectrum while adjusting the magnet position and minimising the magnetic-field component transverse to the NV axis. Similar NV experiments have used this procedure to reduce residual transverse fields below 50 µT.

Permanent magnets change field strength with temperature, so the magnet is temperature stabilized to prevent resonance frequencies drifting during operation. The exact setpoint will be chosen after the measurement of magnetic-field drift vs magnet temperature; we will then regulate the magnet with a temperature sensor, heater and PID controller.

The external neodymium magnet is temperature-stabilized using an RS PRO 4-wire Class A PT100 sensor mounted in thermal contact with the magnet holder, an RS PRO 50 x 50 mm, 3.75 W silicone heater pad attached to the holder, and an RS PRO ET2011 PID controller. The heater is powered from a MEAN WELL HDR-15-12 12 V, 15 W supply.

## 5. Cooling and optical environment

In place of a bulky cryostat, the diamond QPU uses a triple Peltier stack for heat dissipation. Three thermoelectric stages cool the diamond package; heat is dumped through semiconductor heat dissipators on the hot side of the stack.

The diamond-and-ASIC assembly is mounted on the cold plate. The magnet and electrical connections remain accessible around the stack. Exact TEC modules, ΔT and dissipator sizing are fixed after a thermal budget for the ASIC, the photonic load and the 515 nm diode.

**All excitation and collection goes through the on-chip silicon photonic circuit.**

One RF line carries the combined microwave and nuclear-spin RF signal from the external diplexer to the ASIC; a second line is retained as a spare/debug channel. The 515 nm diode is coupled into the chip; collected fluorescence leaves the chip to the SPAD.

## 6. Electronic control

The central control system is an RFSoC4x2 frequency generation module, running QICK-DAWG as the control software. ‘Frequency generation’ here encompasses deterministic pulse sequencing, waveform generation, experiment timing and also synchronization with the optical system.

The RFSoC4x2 generates the microwave waveform, the nuclear-control waveforms, and the experiment timing. Nuclear-control tones sit in the 0.1–10 MHz band. Both paths share the board clock, so relative timing and phase are native to one instrument.

The software must be capable of specifying commands of the form:

At **t = 124 ns**, execute:

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Frequency | 2.873421 GHz |
| Phase | 37° |
| Envelope | Square |
| Duration | 32 ns |

alongside synchronized optical and detector operations.

The control stack coordinates the complete experimental sequence from microwave and RF frequency, phase, amplitude, pulse shape and duration; delays between pulses; 515 nm diode gating; photon-counting windows; and the number and timing of repeated experimental shots. That stack exists to put Pauli X, Y, Z and entangling gates onto the electron and nuclear spins as timed pulses.

## 7. Microwave and RF chain

The two electrical control paths begin separately, before being merged at the diplexer and addressed together. Microwave pulses rotate the electron; RF pulses rotate the nuclei. Together they are the Pauli gates and the entangling gates.

### Microwave path

![Microwave path from the RFSoC 4x2 through the amplifier, switch and diplexer to the sample RF interface.](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/mw-flow.png)

The microwave path controls the NV electron spin. At zero magnetic field the NV electron transition sits at approximately 2.87 GHz, but with the ~40 mT bias field the lower Zeeman branch moves to approximately 1.75 GHz. Therefore, this is the transition we drive.

The RFSoC4x2 generates the ~1.75 GHz waveform directly, with control over frequency, phase, amplitude and pulse timing. No separate microwave up-conversion stage is required because this frequency sits within the RFSoC output range.

In order to suppress DAC images and out-of-band noise before amplification, the signal is then passed through a band-pass filter (Mini-Circuits VBFZ-1690-S+).

The now-filtered signal is sent to the microwave amplifier (Mini-Circuits ZHL-1724HLN+), which provides approximately 36 dB of gain and can deliver roughly +26 dBm (0.4 W) before 1 dB compression across 1.7–2.4 GHz. The drive amplitude is calibrated until the NV reaches our target ~5–10 MHz electron Rabi frequency. The required amplifier output therefore depends on the measured losses through the downstream switch, diplexer, coax and ASIC interconnect.

After amplification, the signal passes through a microwave switch (Mini-Circuits ZFSWA2-63DR+). The switch is opened only during microwave pulses which prevents broadband amplifier noise from continuously reaching the NV during free-evolution periods.

The microwave signal is then sent into the high-frequency port of the diplexer (Mini-Circuits ZDPLX-2150-S+). The nuclear-spin RF path enters the low-frequency port of the same diplexer, and both RF+MW share a single line from this point onwards.

The combined signal then passes through a DC block (Mini-Circuits BLK-89-S+) to prevent unwanted DC offsets from reaching the diamond while allowing both the nuclear-control signals and the ~1.75 GHz electron-control signal to pass.

### RF path

![RF path from the RFSoC 4x2 through the switch, amplifier, low-pass filter and diplexer to the sample RF interface.](https://thenewcomputers.com/images/rf-flow.png)

The RF path controls the intrinsic ^14N spin and the nearby ^13C nuclear spins. We expect to operate primarily from roughly hundreds of kHz to a few MHz.

The RFSoC4x2 generates the nuclear-control waveforms with programmable frequency, phase, amplitude and envelope. Its output passes through the Mini-Circuits ZASWA2-50DR-FA RF switch, followed by the RF amplifier, low-pass filter and diplexer. The amplifier and filter must cover the complete measured nuclear-control band.

The switched signal is then passed through an RF amplifier; the exact amplifier remains TBD until we simulate the ASIC traces and measure the RF field required at the NV. The selection criterion is the power required to reach our target nuclear Rabi rates without exceeding the thermal or power-handling limits of the diplexer or the flip-chip interconnect.

After amplification, the signal also passes through a low-pass filter to remove DAC images and higher-frequency amplifier noise while preserving the nuclear-control band. The exact filter cutoff remains TBD until the complete measured ^14N/^13C frequency range is known.

The conditioned RF signal is then connected to the low-frequency port of the Mini-Circuits ZDPLX-2150-S+ diplexer. This port covers DC–10 MHz. [Manufacturer specification](https://www.minicircuits.com/WebStore/dashboard.html?model=ZDPLX-2150-S%2B).

## 8. Optical Excitation

A 515 nm diode laser drives the NV through the on-chip photonic circuit. Charge repump, electron initialization and fluorescence readout all use this beam. A 637 nm laser is not required. An AOM is not required: the diode is gated electrically by the RFSoC.

The diode model and the coupler onto the chip remain TBD. Drive current and electrical gating must be fast enough for the initialization and readout windows we use in experiment. Comparable NV work initializes the electron with a few microseconds of ~150 µW green light; we calibrate power at the NV rather than assuming that figure.

Before the chip, the beam passes through a Thorlabs NDC-25C-4M variable neutral-density filter for 0–4 OD of attenuation so that the power launched into the waveguide can be calibrated without changing the rest of the path.

On-chip waveguides deliver 515 nm to the selected NV. There is no free-space objective in the operating excitation path. Throughput is set by diode-to-chip coupling and waveguide loss to the NV, and is measured after the photonic circuit is fabricated.

## 9. Optical readout

Fluorescence is collected on-chip and routed off the ASIC to the detector. A free-space objective is not required for readout.

The readout does not require spectrally indistinguishable photons; it only requires enough spin-dependent fluorescence to distinguish the NV electron state. We therefore collect the broad ~650–800 nm phonon sideband, which contains most of the NV emission, rather than isolating the 637 nm zero-phonon line. No 637 nm laser is used.

Residual 515 nm in the collection waveguide must be rejected before the detector while the phonon sideband is transmitted. A Semrock BLP01-647R-25 long-pass filter sits on that path. At 515 nm it provides OD > 6, while transmitting >93% of the fluorescence above 665 nm.

A Thorlabs AC254-050-B-ML, 50 mm achromatic doublet focuses the filtered light onto an Excelitas SPCM-AQRH-10 silicon SPAD. The detector covers 400–1060 nm, has ~65% photon-detection efficiency at 650 nm, a 24 ns dead time and a maximum specified dark-count rate of 1500 counts per second.

Each detected photon produces a TTL pulse. Rather than adding a separate photon counter, that output is connected directly to an RFSoC4x2 ADC input, which QICK-DAWG already supports in photon-counting mode. The RFSoC opens a defined readout window synchronized with each 515 nm pulse and counts the arriving detector pulses during that interval.

Bright- and dark-state reference measurements establish the photon-count distributions and calibrate state assignment. Experiments average counts over repeated 515 nm preparations to estimate spin observables.

## 10. Preparation and readout

The 515 nm diode, delivered through the on-chip photonic circuit, restores the NV’s negative charge state and is used for electron-spin preparation and fluorescence readout. A 637 nm laser is not required.

The electron is prepared in m_s = 0. Each ^13C nucleus is then initialized by transferring the electron’s polarization through two conditional gates: first a nuclear-controlled electron flip, then an electron-controlled nuclear flip. The electron is optically reset afterwards. This sequence is repeated for each selected carbon, preserving the nuclei already prepared.

The intrinsic ^14N qubit uses the m_I = −1 and m_I = 0 states. A nitrogen-selective microwave pulse followed by electron readout identifies the desired starting state. Preparation is repeated until that state is confirmed; population in the unused m_I = +1 state is measured separately.

For measurement, basis-rotation pulses and a conditional gate map the selected nuclear observable onto the electron. 515 nm excitation produces spin-dependent fluorescence, collected on-chip and counted by the SPAD. Bright- and dark-state reference measurements calibrate the readout.

Full-register measurements require a calibrated readout order and protection of nuclei awaiting measurement. Initial two-qubit experiments use averaged fluorescence under 515 nm excitation.

The microwave and RF preparation sequence follows the [published multi-spin NV register architecture](https://arxiv.org/html/1905.02094v2).

## 11. First complete experiment

The first acceptance experiment prepares and measures an entangled state of the NV electron and one ^13C nucleus. Resonance frequencies, pulse amplitudes, pulse durations and phases are calibrated for the selected pair.

- **Prepare:** Initialize the electron and nucleus in |00⟩, using the preparation sequence above.

- **Create a superposition:** Apply a microwave π/2 pulse to the electron.

- **Entangle:** Apply an electron-controlled nuclear flip, compiled from RF rotations and microwave refocusing pulses. With calibrated phases, this prepares the Bell state (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2.

- **Measure:** Repeat the experiment in three measurement settings to obtain the correlations ⟨XX⟩, ⟨YY⟩ and ⟨ZZ⟩. For each setting, apply the analysis rotations below, then a nuclear-controlled electron flip and optical electron readout.

| Correlation | Analysis rotation applied to both qubits |
| --- | --- |
| XX | R y (−π/2) |
| YY | R x (+π/2) |
| ZZ | None |

The Bell-state fidelity is

F = (1 + ⟨XX⟩ − ⟨YY⟩ + ⟨ZZ⟩) / 4

The experiment passes when the lower 95% confidence bound exceeds 0.5, including uncertainty from readout calibration and analysis pulses. Results include the three correlations, fidelity, uncertainty and calibration settings.

## 12. User interface and API

The user should not be required to understand any of the microwave, RF, optical or FPGA hardware to operate the machine.

All Diamond QPU units should appear from the user perspective as straight-out-the-box and a delight to use. The absolute minimum amount of clicks should be required to open up the intuitive user interface.

The primary interface will therefore be a Python SDK with first-class Qiskit compatibility.

A user should be able to:

- Connect to the machine.

- Query available qubits.

- Click on a picture of an individual qubit at any arbitrary point in the circuit and see its state vector on the Bloch sphere.

- Retrieve detailed calibration information, but only if specifically requested.

- Submit quantum circuits.

- Specify shot count.

- Run the circuits.

The intended workflow is approximately:

```
from pathfinder import PathfinderProvider
from qiskit import transpile

provider = PathfinderProvider()
backend = provider.get_backend("diamond_qpu")

circuit = transpile(circuit, backend)
job = backend.run(circuit, shots=1000)

result = job.result()
```

The Pathfinder backend exposes its native gate set, available qubits, connectivity, timing constraints and current calibration data to the transpiler. The native gates are the same operations as everywhere else in this document: Pauli X, Y, Z and entangling pulses on the spins.
